lesson.title: The Fading Signal: Transient Response and the Time Constant
lesson.summary: Transient response is the temporary, decaying portion of a circuit's behavior that appears right after a sudden change and dies out exponentially, governed entirely by the circuit's time constant. It is the bridge between where a circuit starts and the steady state it is heading toward.
lesson.body:
Steady-state response tells you where a circuit ends up. Transient response tells you the story of how it gets there. The moment a switch closes, a source turns on, or any sudden change disturbs a circuit containing a capacitor or inductor, the circuit cannot jump instantly to its new steady-state value. Capacitor voltage and inductor current must change continuously, so there is an in-between period where the response overshoots, undershoots, or simply eases toward its final value. That in-between period, and specifically the extra piece of the response that is not part of the steady-state value, is the transient response, and it always takes the shape of a decaying exponential in a simple RL or RC circuit.

The speed of that decay is set by a single number called the time constant, written as tau. For an RC circuit, tau = RC, and for an RL circuit, tau = L/R. The transient term always looks like K times e raised to the power of negative t over tau, where K is whatever amount is left over once you subtract the steady-state value from the initial value. After one time constant, the transient has decayed to about 36.8 percent of its starting size (e^-1 = 0.3679). After five time constants, it has shrunk to under 1 percent, which is why five tau is the standard rule of thumb for calling a circuit "settled."

Consider a series RC circuit with R = 10 kilo-ohms and C = 100 nanofarads, driven by a 5 V step with the capacitor initially uncharged. The time constant is tau = RC = 10,000 ohms x 100 x 10^-9 F = 1 x 10^-3 seconds, or 1 millisecond. The full response is v(t) = 5 - 5e^(-t/0.001), where the "5" is the steady-state piece (capacitor fully charged to the source voltage, matching what steady-state response predicts) and the "-5e^(-t/0.001)" is the transient piece by itself.

Isolate just that transient piece at t = 2 milliseconds, which is two time constants: the transient magnitude is 5 x e^-2 = 5 x 0.1353 = 0.6767 V. So the total voltage at that instant is 5 - 0.6767 = 4.323 V, meaning the circuit has already closed about 86 percent of the gap between its start and its finish, even though two time constants is a small fraction of the total settling time. This is the practical payoff of understanding the transient piece separately: you can quote exactly how much "leftover disturbance" remains at any moment, not just the total voltage.

The same exponential shape governs RL circuits, just with tau = L/R substituted for tau = RC. A circuit built from L = 100 millihenries and R = 100 ohms has tau = 0.1/100 = 1 millisecond, decaying at exactly the same rate as the RC example above even though the underlying physical mechanism, a collapsing magnetic field instead of a draining capacitor, is completely different. That is the deeper reason the transient term is worth studying on its own: the same math describes very different hardware, as long as you know which time constant formula applies.

Everything from here forward is built on this idea. Final conditions and forced response identify the steady-state destination; natural response and the time constant describe the fading transient; and complete response, step response, and pulse response are all just different ways of assembling the transient term and the steady-state term into one full description of circuit behavior over time.
